title: Untangling a Bad Habit
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Drawing on habit researcher B.J. Fogg, this article reframes bad-habit change as untangling a knotted rope rather than yanking on it all at once. It explains why pulling on the whole rope of a habit like overthinking backfires, and instead breaks the habit into smaller sub-habits that can be tackled individually. The suggested strategy is to isolate and eliminate the easiest sub-habit first to build momentum before addressing the harder ones. It's a practical model for leaders trying to help themselves or team members change entrenched behavior without becoming overwhelmed.
points: Bad habits provoke shame and guilt in ways good habits don't, making avoidance easier than confrontation.
Fogg's rope metaphor: pulling on an entire tangled habit at once usually makes things worse.
A broad habit like 'overthinking' is really a bundle of smaller sub-habits that can be isolated.
Picking the easiest knot to untangle first builds momentum and confidence for tackling harder ones.
Eradicating a bad habit means reducing it to its component parts rather than attacking it as a whole.
quotes: He warns that pulling on the entire rope usually makes things worse, especially in the long run.
After multiple failed attempts to change a bad habit, people give up and give in, often exacerbating the consequences of the negative choice.
The key is to realize that the abstraction of a bad habit (such as overthinking problems) is full of a subset of smaller actions or habits.
Fogg suggests picking the one easiest sub-habit to change as a way to create momentum and confidence going forward.
Reducing a bad habit to its fundamental elements and addressing them is how good leaders kill bad habits.
